newsitem.title: USA: Santa Fe offer seen oversubscribed, priced at top.
newsitem.headline: Santa Fe offer seen oversubscribed, priced at top.

text.p: The offering of 30 million shares in contract driller Santa Fe International Corp is expected to be oversubscribed, perhaps as much as eight times, analysts said.
The shares being sold by the Kuwait Petroleum Corp will be priced on Monday between $24-$27 in a deal which trading sources familiar with the transcation said had been "heavily oversubscribed".
One fund manager said that with such a high profile deal, it was likely Santa Fe would be priced at the top end or even above the indicated range.
"They have already increased the share count and are likely to be as greedy as they can," he said.
The company operates 51 offshore and land rigs in 16 countries and has the largest fleet of heavy duty harsh environment jackup rigs in the world plus three deepwater semisubmerible rigs.

"Santa Fe is a high-quality offering and will be a huge, liquid stock which investors expect will trade up on its first day, so they are putting in big orders," said Ravi Kamath, analyst at Jefferies & Co.
The deal is being lead managed by Goldman Sachs with 24 million shares offered in the U.S. and six million overseas.
After the issue, KPC will own 70 percent of the stock.
Analysts said that the drilling sector was set to receive a boost from funds as visible earnings growth from other industry sectors, such as technology stocks, slows.
"Once investors see that that earnings growth among the drillers will continue even with weaker oil prices, they will increase allocations," said Iain Smith, analyst at Rodman & Renshaw.
The fund manager said that he also thought that the sector was attractive.
"Dayrates for rigs are high and Santa Fe looks very well positioned," he said.
Dayrates for drilling rigs have risen sharply, Ensco International reported this week that it had struck a deal for a Gulf of Mexico jackup rig at $80,000.

In the harsh deepwater and the semisubmersible sector capacity utilization is 100 percent and although that prompted fears of new builds, analysts say that it will be at least two years before any significant capacity would come on. ((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
